lists.title: Latin A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: First Latin: the nominative/accusative case pair, the first and second declensions, the irregular verb sum, first-conjugation present tense, adjective agreement, the two-way preposition in, and why word order is flexible.

points.title: Nominative and accusative: subject and direct object
points.function: Tell who does the action from who or what receives it
points.explanation: Latin marks a noun's job in the sentence with its ENDING, not its position. The subject (who's doing it) takes the nominative case; the direct object (what's acted on) takes the accusative. Puella becomes puellam when it's the object: Puella puerum amat ("The girl loves the boy") vs. Puer puellam amat ("The boy loves the girl") — swap the endings and the meaning flips, even if you also swap the word order.

points.title: First declension nouns: -a / -ae feminine
points.function: Recognize and form the most common noun pattern
points.explanation: Most first-declension nouns are feminine and end -a in the nominative singular (puella, aqua, terra, insula). The genitive singular ends -ae, which gives the whole declension its name and means "of the ___": puellae = "of the girl" / "the girl's." The accusative singular ends -am: puella → puellam.

drills.translation: The girl lives on the island.

points.title: Second declension nouns: -us masculine and -um neuter
points.function: Learn the other core noun pattern
points.explanation: Second-declension nouns end -us (masculine, like dominus) or -um (neuter, like bellum) in the nominative. Neuter nouns are special: their nominative and accusative forms are IDENTICAL — bellum stays bellum whether it's the subject or the object. Only masculine and feminine nouns change shape between the two.

drills.hint: war — neuter, same form for subject or object
war — neuter object looks just like the subject form

points.title: sum, esse — the irregular verb "to be"
points.function: Say what something or someone IS
points.explanation: Sum ("I am") is Latin's most irregular verb, just as "to be" is irregular in English: sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt. Sum takes no direct object — instead of an accusative, it links right back to the nominative: Puella bona est ("The girl is good"), not puellam.

drills.hint: we are — 1st person plural of sum
you are — 2nd person singular of sum

points.title: First conjugation present tense (-are verbs)
points.function: Conjugate the largest family of Latin verbs
points.explanation: Verbs like amo ("I love") belong to the first conjugation, spotted by the -are infinitive (amare). The present tense endings are -o, -as, -at, -amus, -atis, -ant, added to the stem ama-: amo, amas, amat, amamus, amatis, amant. Because the ending already shows the person, Latin usually drops the pronoun.

drills.hint: I love — 1st person singular, no pronoun needed

points.title: Adjective-noun agreement
points.function: Match adjective endings to the noun they describe
points.explanation: Latin adjectives change their ending to match the noun's gender, number, and case: magnus (masculine), magna (feminine), and magnum (neuter) all mean "big." Puella magna and dominus magnus both mean "big," but the ending has to match the Latin noun, not the English word.

points.title: Prepositions: in + accusative vs. in + ablative
points.explanation: The preposition in changes meaning with the case that follows it: in + accusative means motion INTO (in insulam = "into the island"), while in + ablative means location IN or ON (in insula = "on the island"). Same preposition, different case, different meaning — a pattern Latin uses with several two-way prepositions.

drills.translation: The girl lives on the island.
The boy comes onto the island.
The water is on the land.

points.title: Word order: Latin puts case marking to work
points.function: Understand why word order is flexible in Latin
points.explanation: Because endings — not position — show who does what, Latin word order is flexible for emphasis, though the neutral default is Subject-Object-Verb: Puella puerum amat, literally "girl boy loves." Puerum puella amat and Amat puella puerum mean the same thing; only the endings, never the order, decide who loves whom.

drills.translation: The girl loves the boy. (default subject-object-verb order)
drills.hint: loves — verb comes last in the neutral order

drills.translation: The girl loves the boy. (verb fronted for emphasis)
drills.hint: loves — same verb, moved to the front

drills.translation: The girl loves the boy. (object fronted)
drills.hint: girl — the subject can move without changing meaning, thanks to its ending
